_comment: Parkinsonism is a SHORT CASE: a movement-disorder syndrome examined mostly through observation (posture, tremor, gait) rather than a full systemic workup. Structured like anaemia.json: no systemic_exam/past_personal_drug_family/summary/treatment chapters. Built almost entirely on the shared skill.exam.neuro.tone_power and skill.exam.neuro.gait, with emphasis overlays, plus the genuinely new content: tremor character, bradykinesia, and the secondary-versus-idiopathic distinction.

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: A typical presentation is a tremor of one hand at rest, noticed first by a family member or when the limb is relaxed, together with a vague sense of slowness or stiffness that has crept in over months to years.

chapters.title: General and movement examination
chapters.blurb: Watch before you touch: the face and the posture say most of it

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Look for the mask-like face with reduced blinking, a stooped posture, and reduced spontaneous movement before the patient has said a word. Watch the hands at rest in the lap for a pill-rolling tremor while you are still taking the history.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Check the blood pressure lying and then standing. A significant drop on standing (orthostatic hypotension) is a common non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease and is also the red flag that first raises multiple system atrophy instead.

skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.expect: Expect 'lead-pipe' rigidity, increased tone through the WHOLE range of passive movement, unlike the tone of an upper motor neurone lesion which peaks and then gives way. When a tremor is superimposed on this rigidity it becomes ratchet-like, cogwheel rigidity, most easily felt at the wrist while distracting the patient with movement of the other limb. Power itself is normal; this is a movement disorder, not a weakness.

skill.exam.neuro.gait.expect: Expect a stooped, shuffling, festinant gait: small, flat-footed steps that hurry to catch up with the forward-tipped centre of gravity, reduced arm swing (often asymmetrical, worse on the more affected side), difficulty initiating the first step, and freezing at doorways or turns. Retropulsion, small involuntary backward steps when gently pushed from in front while stopped, is a specific test worth doing deliberately.

stations.title: Examine this patient's gait and tremor
stations.task: This 68-year-old man's family have noticed a tremor in his right hand and that he has become slower over the last year. Examine him and present your findings.
examinerQuestions: How would you deliberately bring out cogwheel rigidity if it is not obvious at rest?
Name two features that would make you suspect a Parkinson-plus syndrome rather than idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
This patient started a new antiemetic three months before the tremor began. Does that change your thinking?

cases.title: A retired clerk whose handwriting has shrunk
cases.opening: Subhash Rao, 68, has come to the neurology outpatient department with his daughter. He sits quietly in the chair with his right hand resting and trembling gently in his lap, his face still and unblinking. Introduce yourself and take a history.
cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean, doctor. Can you ask that a different way?

patient.name: Subhash Rao
patient.residence: Urban, lives with his wife and daughter

presenting.reply: Doctor, my daughter noticed my right hand shaking about a year ago, when I am just sitting. Lately I have also become slow, and my handwriting has become very small.

tremor_character.reply: It is worst when my hand is just resting on my lap or the armrest, doctor. If I pick up my tea cup, it almost stops.

tremor_side.reply: It started in my right hand only. In the last two or three months my left hand has started doing it a little too, but the right is still much worse.

slowness.reply: Everything takes longer now. Buttoning my shirt, getting up from the chair. My daughter says my handwriting has become tiny, I did not notice it myself until she showed me an old letter.

gait_voice_face.reply: My wife says I walk with smaller steps now and that my face does not show expression the way it used to. My voice has become a bit softer too. I have not fallen.

drug_history.reply: No, I am not on any tablet for vomiting or for my nerves. Only a tablet for blood pressure, been on it for ten years, no change recently.

autonomic.reply: I do get a little constipated, doctor, but no fainting or dizziness when I stand up. No trouble with urination.

smell.reply: Now that you ask, my sense of smell has been poor for a few years, even before the shaking started. I thought it was just old age.

mood_sleep.reply: I have felt a bit low sometimes, but nothing I would call depression. My sleep is alright, though my wife says I sometimes talk in my sleep.

family.reply: No one else in the family has had a tremor or Parkinson's that I know of.

comorbidity.reply: Just the blood pressure, well controlled. No diabetes, no thyroid problem, no operations.

functional_impact.reply: I can still dress and eat by myself, just slower. I retired eight years ago, well before any of this started, so it has not affected my work.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Mask-like facial expression with reduced blinking. Stooped posture. Right hand shows a 4 to 6 Hz resting tremor with a pill-rolling character that reduces on voluntary movement. Reduced spontaneous movement generally.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Blood pressure 132/82 lying, 126/78 standing after two minutes, no symptomatic drop. Pulse 78 regular. No postural symptoms.

skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.finding: Lead-pipe rigidity at both wrists, right more than left, with a superimposed cogwheel quality on the right when the other limb is moved. Power full and symmetrical in all limbs, 5/5 throughout.

skill.exam.neuro.gait.finding: Stooped, shuffling gait with small, flat-footed steps. Reduced right arm swing, left relatively preserved. Slow to initiate the first step. No freezing observed. Mild retropulsion on the pull test, recovers in two steps.

clinical_diagnosis.label: Clinical assessment (history and examination)
clinical_diagnosis.result: Asymmetric-onset rest tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia with a shuffling gait and no red flags for a secondary cause or Parkinson-plus syndrome.
clinical_diagnosis.note: This is what makes the diagnosis. Idiopathic Parkinson's disease has no confirmatory blood test or routine scan.

drug_review.label: Medication review
drug_review.result: No dopamine receptor blocking drugs, antiemetics or antipsychotics in the current or recent drug history.
drug_review.note: Excludes drug-induced parkinsonism, which is reversible and the single most important mimic to rule out.

orthostatic_bp.label: Lying and standing blood pressure
orthostatic_bp.note: Screens for early, prominent autonomic failure, which would raise multiple system atrophy instead of idiopathic disease.

mri_brain.label: MRI brain
mri_brain.note: Not indicated here: no red flags such as early falls, prominent early autonomic failure, or marked early symmetry. Imaging is reserved for atypical features, not ordered as a routine confirmatory test in a classic presentation.

serum_ceruloplasmin.label: Serum caeruloplasmin
serum_ceruloplasmin.note: Not indicated at 68 years old. This test is for Wilson's disease, which is a consideration in a new movement disorder under about 40, not here.

dopaminergic_trial.label: Trial of dopaminergic therapy
dopaminergic_trial.note: A sustained response would support the diagnosis, but this is a therapeutic decision for the treating specialist, not a bedside confirmatory test to order today.

differentialModel.answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease. Consider drug-induced parkinsonism, vascular parkinsonism, essential tremor and a Parkinson-plus syndrome such as progressive supranuclear palsy or multiple system atrophy.

diagnosis.answer: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease, asymmetric right-sided rest tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia with no red flags for a secondary cause or Parkinson-plus syndrome, functionally Hoehn and Yahr stage II.

managementModel.answer: Confirm the diagnosis clinically, actively exclude a drug cause and red flags for Parkinson-plus disease, then start dopaminergic therapy chosen for his age and functional needs. Alongside drug treatment: patient and family education, physiotherapy and gait training, a falls-risk assessment, and screening for non-motor features such as constipation, mood and sleep. Regular review to track progression and treatment response.

teachingPoints: The story is told before he says a word: an unblinking face and a hand trembling at rest while he sits waiting. Observation starts the moment you see the patient, not when you start asking questions.

Asymmetry is the single most useful early feature here. It began in the right hand alone and only recently touched the left, which is exactly the pattern idiopathic disease should follow, and it argues against a Parkinson-plus syndrome or a toxic cause that would usually be symmetrical from the start.
The tremor going quiet when he lifts his tea cup is not a trivial detail, it is the defining behaviour of a rest tremor, and distinguishes it immediately from an action or intention tremor.

Power is completely normal. Rigidity and bradykinesia can look like weakness to an unwary student, but this is a movement disorder, not a motor neurone or muscle problem, and confirming full power is part of making the diagnosis, not an afterthought.

Hyposmia for years before the tremor, and sleep talking his wife noticed, are non-motor features that predated the motor disease. They matter both diagnostically and because they affect his life as much as the shaking does.
A completely normal drug history and no postural drop are not throwaway negatives. They are what let you commit to idiopathic disease rather than a reversible or Parkinson-plus alternative.
There is no scan or blood test that confirms this diagnosis. The MRI and the caeruloplasmin were left undone deliberately, because nothing in this history or exam suggested reaching for them.

skill.pd.basics.title: What parkinsonism is
skill.pd.basics.oneLine: A syndrome first, a disease second: idiopathic Parkinson's is only one cause of it
skill.pd.basics.why: Students routinely use 'Parkinson's disease' and 'parkinsonism' interchangeably. Parkinsonism is the clinical syndrome; idiopathic Parkinson's disease is its single most common cause, but treating every parkinsonian patient as automatically having Parkinson's disease is how a reversible drug-induced case, or a more aggressive Parkinson-plus syndrome, gets missed.
skill.pd.basics.body: Parkinsonism is a clinical syndrome of bradykinesia plus at least one of rest tremor or rigidity, with the classic gait and postural change that follow from them. It has many causes; idiopathic Parkinson's disease is the most common.
keyPoints: The core motor features are bradykinesia (slowness and poverty of movement), rest tremor, rigidity, and postural instability with a characteristic gait.

Onset in idiopathic Parkinson's disease is always ASYMMETRICAL, one side affected more than, and usually before, the other, becoming bilateral only within a year or so; a patient with symmetrical onset from the very start should make you think of a secondary cause or a Parkinson-plus syndrome instead.

Non-motor features are just as much a part of the disease as the tremor: autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension, constipation, urinary symptoms), neuropsychiatric features (depression, anxiety, later dementia), sleep disorders, and a reduced sense of smell that can precede the motor signs by years.
Reduced sense of smell (hyposmia) preceding the motor signs is a genuinely useful early clue and is worth asking about specifically.
pitfalls: Assuming symmetrical-onset tremor at presentation is still typical idiopathic disease.
Treating the non-motor features as incidental rather than as part of the same diagnosis, and so missing the autonomic and psychiatric burden of the disease.

probes.q: Name the core motor features of the parkinsonian syndrome.
probes.a: Bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity, and postural instability with a characteristic gait.

probes.q: Is idiopathic Parkinson's disease typically symmetrical or asymmetrical at onset?
probes.a: Asymmetrical, one side more affected than the other, becoming bilateral within about a year.

probes.q: Give two non-motor features of Parkinson's disease that can precede the motor signs.
probes.a: Reduced sense of smell (hyposmia) and sleep disturbance (such as REM sleep behaviour disorder) are both recognised to precede the motor signs, sometimes by years.

skill.pd.signs.title: The parkinsonian picture
skill.pd.signs.oneLine: Four signs from one problem, plus the paradox that briefly cancels all of them
skill.pd.signs.why: Recognising that rigidity, bradykinesia, the mask face and the shuffling gait are different expressions of the same basal ganglia dysfunction, rather than an unlinked checklist, is what lets a student recognise the syndrome quickly and explain it coherently in a viva.
skill.pd.signs.body: Put the bedside findings together as one syndrome, and know the specific bedside signs that go beyond the basic triad.
keyPoints: Myerson's sign: repetitive tapping over the glabella at about 2 Hz produces a SUSTAINED blink response in parkinsonism, where a normal subject habituates and stops blinking after the first few taps.

Kinesia paradoxa: a striking, well-documented phenomenon in which a patient who is usually markedly bradykinetic or even seemingly frozen can, under sudden need or strong emotional stimulus, briefly walk or even run normally. It illustrates that the problem is one of movement INITIATION rather than a fixed loss of the ability to move.
Widened palpebral fissures, infrequent blinking, and a fixed, mask-like facial expression (hypomimia) are part of the same bradykinesia affecting facial musculature.
The postural change, a stooped, flexed posture of the trunk, neck and limbs, together with reduced righting reflexes, is what underlies both the festinant gait and the tendency to fall forward.
None of these signs alone makes the diagnosis; the combination, together with asymmetry at onset, is what does.
pitfalls: Testing the glabellar tap only once or twice, rather than repetitively, and so missing the failure to habituate.
Interpreting kinesia paradoxa as evidence the patient is exaggerating their disability, when it is a recognised feature of the disease itself.
Describing the face as 'flat affect' without recognising it as hypomimia, a motor sign, not a mood sign.

probes.a: A sustained blink response to repetitive glabellar tapping, where a normal subject habituates and stops blinking after a few taps.

probes.q: Describe kinesia paradoxa and what it tells you about the underlying problem.
probes.a: A patient who is usually markedly bradykinetic can, under sudden need or emotional stress, briefly move normally, walking or even running. It shows the deficit is fundamentally one of movement initiation rather than a fixed structural inability to move.

rubric.text: Correctly elicits and interprets the glabellar tap
Links rigidity, bradykinesia, facial and postural findings as one syndrome rather than a list

skill.pd.differential.title: Idiopathic, secondary, or Parkinson-plus
skill.pd.differential.oneLine: The tremor looks the same; the red flags that separate the three do not
skill.pd.differential.why: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease, a reversible secondary parkinsonism, and a Parkinson-plus syndrome all present with the same core triad but have entirely different prognoses and treatment responses, and the discriminating features are specific, examinable red flags rather than a gut feeling.
skill.pd.differential.body: Screen for secondary causes first, since some are reversible, then screen for Parkinson-plus red flags, since they change the prognosis and the treatment response even though nothing is reversible.
keyPoints: Secondary (reversible or treatable) parkinsonism: dopamine receptor blocking drugs (antiemetics, antipsychotics), vascular (multi-infarct) parkinsonism, normal pressure hydrocephalus, Wilson's disease in a young patient, and toxin exposure. A drug history and a careful search for a gait-cognition-incontinence triad (hydrocephalus) or a young age of onset (Wilson's) are the key screens.
Progressive supranuclear palsy: early falls, restricted downward gaze, and a characteristic startled or 'reptilian' stare; a poor or absent response to standard dopaminergic therapy is typical.
Multiple system atrophy: parkinsonism together with early, prominent autonomic failure (marked orthostatic hypotension, urinary symptoms) and/or cerebellar signs.
Corticobasal degeneration: markedly asymmetric, with apraxia, cortical sensory loss, or an alien-limb phenomenon in one hand.
Dementia with Lewy bodies: early, prominent visual hallucinations and cognitive fluctuation, with dementia appearing early rather than late as it can in longstanding idiopathic disease.
Idiopathic Parkinson's disease remains the default once these are screened for and excluded: asymmetric onset, a classic rest tremor, and a good, sustained response to dopaminergic treatment.
pitfalls: Not screening the drug history before assuming a new parkinsonism is idiopathic.
Missing early falls or an eye-movement abnormality that would suggest progressive supranuclear palsy.
Attributing early, severe autonomic failure or hallucinations to 'just Parkinson's' rather than considering multiple system atrophy or Lewy body disease specifically.
Forgetting Wilson's disease in a young patient with any new movement disorder.

probes.q: Name two features that would raise suspicion of a Parkinson-plus syndrome rather than idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
probes.a: Early falls with restricted downward gaze (progressive supranuclear palsy); early, prominent autonomic failure or cerebellar signs (multiple system atrophy); marked early asymmetry with apraxia or alien-limb phenomenon (corticobasal degeneration); or early hallucinations and cognitive fluctuation (dementia with Lewy bodies).

probes.q: A 70-year-old with new gait difficulty, urinary incontinence and mild cognitive slowing. What treatable cause should be actively considered before labelling this Parkinson's disease?
probes.a: Normal pressure hydrocephalus, given the classic triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment.

rubric.text: Screens for a reversible secondary cause, especially drugs
Names at least one red flag for a Parkinson-plus syndrome

skill.ix.pd.workup.title: Investigating a new parkinsonism
skill.ix.pd.workup.oneLine: This is a clinical diagnosis; every test here is looking for an exception
skill.ix.pd.workup.why: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease has no confirmatory blood test or routine scan finding, and understanding that changes how a student should think about investigations here: not as a route to the diagnosis, but as a targeted search for the secondary and Parkinson-plus causes that would change the plan.
skill.ix.pd.workup.body: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease is diagnosed clinically. Investigations are ordered to exclude the alternatives suggested by the history, examination and red flags, not to confirm the diagnosis itself.
keyPoints: In a typical, asymmetric-onset, older patient with a classic rest tremor and no red flags, imaging is often not required to make the clinical diagnosis.

MRI brain is indicated where a red flag is present: early falls, prominent early autonomic failure, marked early symmetry, or an atypical course, and can show findings supporting a specific Parkinson-plus syndrome, such as characteristic midbrain or pontine atrophy patterns, or can show vascular change supporting a vascular parkinsonism.
Serum caeruloplasmin and a slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings are indicated in any patient with onset before about 40 years, to look for Wilson's disease, which is treatable.

A thorough medication review is itself an investigation here: identifying and, where possible with the prescriber's involvement, withdrawing an implicated dopamine receptor blocking drug can be diagnostic as well as therapeutic.

A clear, sustained response to a trial of dopaminergic therapy supports the diagnosis of idiopathic disease, while a poor or absent response should prompt reconsideration of a Parkinson-plus syndrome; this response is assessed and interpreted by the treating specialist, not used casually as a bedside test.
pitfalls: Ordering an MRI reflexively in every new parkinsonism when the clinical picture is entirely typical and there are no red flags.
Not checking for Wilson's disease in a young patient with a new movement disorder.
Treating a poor response to dopaminergic therapy as proof the patient is not adherent, rather than as a clue toward a Parkinson-plus syndrome.

probes.q: Is idiopathic Parkinson's disease confirmed by a blood test or scan?
probes.a: No. It is a clinical diagnosis; investigations are used to exclude secondary causes and Parkinson-plus syndromes, not to confirm idiopathic disease.

probes.q: A 32-year-old presents with a new tremor and mild rigidity. What must be checked before any other workup?
probes.a: Serum caeruloplasmin and a slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings, to look for Wilson's disease, which is treatable and must not be missed in a young patient with a new movement disorder.

skill.pd.diagnosis.title: Stating the diagnosis
skill.pd.diagnosis.oneLine: Name it, exclude a secondary cause, and stage it functionally
skill.pd.diagnosis.why: 'Parkinson's disease' alone tells a colleague nothing about how disabled the patient is or how confident the diagnosis is. A complete statement names the type, notes that secondary and Parkinson-plus causes have been actively considered, and stages the functional severity.
skill.pd.diagnosis.body: State the diagnosis in three parts: the type, the confidence (having actively screened for red flags), and the functional stage.
keyPoints: Type: idiopathic Parkinson's disease, secondary (drug-induced, vascular, and so on), or a named Parkinson-plus syndrome.
Confidence: state explicitly that red flags for a secondary cause or a Parkinson-plus syndrome were actively sought and not found, rather than leaving this implicit.

Functional stage, using the Hoehn and Yahr scale: stage I is unilateral involvement only with minimal or no functional impairment; stage II is bilateral or midline involvement without impaired balance; stage III is the first sign of impaired postural (righting) reflexes with mild to moderate disability; stage IV is fully developed, severely disabling disease in a patient who can still stand and walk unassisted; stage V is confinement to a bed or wheelchair unless aided.

A worked example: 'Idiopathic Parkinson's disease, asymmetric right-sided rest tremor and rigidity with no red flags for a secondary cause or Parkinson-plus syndrome on history, examination or drug review; functionally Hoehn and Yahr stage II.'
pitfalls: Writing 'Parkinson's disease' with no functional stage.
Not stating that secondary causes and red flags were actively excluded, leaving the diagnosis unsupported.
Confusing Hoehn and Yahr stage with symptom duration; it measures functional and postural impairment, not how long the patient has had symptoms.

probes.q: What three elements make a complete parkinsonism diagnosis?
probes.a: The type (idiopathic, secondary, or Parkinson-plus), confirmation that red flags were sought and not found, and the functional (Hoehn and Yahr) stage.

probes.q: A patient has bilateral involvement, and the first evidence of impaired postural righting reflexes, with mild to moderate disability. What Hoehn and Yahr stage is this?

rubric.text: States idiopathic, secondary, or Parkinson-plus explicitly
